name: JSON
license: Open standard, free to use; ECMA-404 is also ISO/IEC 21778
summary: The plain-text data format of web APIs: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null, with one small grammar every language can parse.
intro: JSON is a text syntax, not a program. A JSON text is one value: an object (`{"name": value, …}`), an array (`[…]`), a string in double quotes with backslash escapes, a number, `true`, `false` or `null`. That is the whole type system. There are no comments, no dates, no binary data and no `NaN` or `Infinity`. RFC 8259 requires UTF-8 whenever JSON travels between systems that aren’t part of one closed ecosystem, and lets parsers set their own limits on size, nesting depth and the range and precision of numbers. Most use IEEE 754 doubles, so integers are only guaranteed to survive a round trip between −(2^53−1) and 2^53−1. Object names “SHOULD be unique”; when they aren’t, parsers disagree about which value wins.

For data files the usual form is JSON Lines, also called newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON): one JSON value per line in UTF-8, so a file can be appended to, streamed and split without parsing it whole. To describe and validate documents, teams add JSON Schema, a separate specification whose latest version is 2020-12. The syntax itself is defined twice, in IETF RFC 8259 (an Internet Standard) and Ecma’s ECMA-404 (also ISO/IEC 21778), both from December 2017 and kept aligned on purpose. Anyone can use it for free, and every mainstream language ships a parser.
strengths: Parsers for practically every language (json.org lists dozens), and built into JavaScript since ECMAScript 5
Maps directly onto the objects or dictionaries and arrays or lists that programs already use
A grammar small enough to fit on one page, so documents are easy to read, diff and generate
JSON Lines makes logs and event files append-friendly and streamable, one record per line
limits: No comments, which makes it awkward for hand-edited configuration
Number precision is left to each parser: IDs above 2^53 silently change in JavaScript, so I-JSON (RFC 7493) recommends sending big or exact numbers as strings
No binary or date types: binary goes in base64url strings, about a third bigger than the raw bytes, and dates are strings by convention
Every record repeats its field names as text, and it’s a row format, so analytical scans read everything; convert to Parquet for querying
Duplicate keys, member order and very large numbers are handled differently by different parsers, which RFC 8259 calls out as interoperability problems

story: Data formats at the turn of the century were either ad hoc or modelled on databases and documents, XML above all. Douglas Crockford, then CTO of State Software, found in April 2001 that JavaScript’s own object literals were an ideal way to send data across the network; by his account, several other people discovered the same thing independently. In 2002 he bought the json.org domain and put up a page describing the format as a subset of ECMA-262, 3rd edition.

By his account, it spread with no further effort on his part. In July 2006 Crockford published RFC 4627 to register the `application/json` media type, listing its design goals as “minimal, portable, textual, and a subset of JavaScript.” That December he presented JSON at the XML 2006 conference as “the fat-free alternative to XML.” ECMAScript 5 built a JSON object into the language in 2009, and the syntax became a formal standard twice: ECMA-404 in 2013, and RFC 8259, an Internet Standard aligned with ECMA-404, in December 2017.

choices.why: Browsers could already read it, and its strings, numbers, objects and arrays looked like the data structures of C-family languages, so programmers needed no new model.
Crockford wrote that “no revisions to the JSON grammar are anticipated”, so a JSON text from 2002 still parses today and no reader has to check versions.
To stay minimal, and because JSON “does not want to be tied to any particular internal representation” of numbers. The cost is that precision is left to each parser.
Crockford argued that being well-formed isn’t the same as being correct, so every application has to validate its own input. Schemas came later, from the separate JSON Schema project.
